Meet your teacher

Dynamic yet gentle — just enough of everything

I'm Olivia, a hatha flow teacher trained in Budapest and now teaching in Fort Myers. My classes won't ask you to stand on your hands. They'll ask you to breathe, to notice, and to move with a little more ease than you walked in with.

Every class weaves together breathwork, strength, stretching, balance, a real flow state and an unhurried relaxation at the end. Complete beginners are welcome, and people who have practiced for years still find a challenge.

Most of my students aren't chasing the perfect pose. They come between work, kids, grandkids, golf and gardening — and leave saying things like “I needed that,” “I've finally landed” or “I'm going to sleep so well tonight.” That's the whole point.

What “hatha” means

Ha is the sun. Tha is the moon.

Hatha yoga balances the active and the receptive in us: effort and ease, strength and surrender. When that balance tips, we feel it first as tension or restlessness.

On the mat we use the body to find the balance again. The poses are a doorway to meditation — a more dynamic doorway — and only one of the eight limbs of yoga.

FAQ

Am I flexible enough for yoga?

The question everyone asks first — and a few others.

All questions

Am I flexible enough for yoga?

You don't need to be flexible to start yoga — flexibility is something the practice builds. My classes are for people who, between work, family, grandkids, gardening and everything else, are perfectly happy with “that felt good,” “I've landed,” “I'm going to sleep so well” or “my back doesn't hurt anymore.”

We won't be practicing handstands. Classes are varied and there's always a little challenge in them, but nothing is compulsory.

I'm a complete beginner. Which class should I take?

Beginners are warmly welcome, especially if movement is already part of your life in some way. Slow Flow is the gentlest place to start; Hatha Flow is stronger and more dynamic. If you'd like to learn the foundations first, one or two private sessions are a great way in.

How hard are the group classes?

Everyone finds something different hard. For some it's the strength work, for others the stretching or the balance — and for some, switching off their thoughts for an hour.

Hatha Flow is the stronger, more dynamic class. Slow Flow puts more emphasis on observation, at a slower pace. Both include a flow experience, which for me is the most beautiful part of yoga. Sometimes I hold strengthening poses a little longer so everyone's attention can arrive.

What should I bring?

Comfortable clothes you can move in, a bottle of water, and your own mat if you have a favorite. If you need to borrow one, mention it when you book. We practice barefoot. For beach sessions, bring a large towel or a mat, and sun protection.

About Olivia

Hatha flow teacher, trained in Budapest, teaching in Fort Myers — and a firm believer that nobody on the next mat is watching you.

✺

Yoga found me as exercise. It stayed because it taught me to be here, now.

I came to yoga the way most people do: looking for a good way to move. What I found was a tool for getting to know myself — one that slowly brought up a kind of confidence and self-kindness I hadn't known I was missing. That is what I want to pass on in every class.

If you look at yoga only as a workout, the extra spice is that it's never just about strength. Even the toughest class holds observation, silence and permission. And strength without permission always runs out.

Training and teaching

I earned my hatha yoga teacher certification, recognized by Yoga Alliance International, in 2023 at Samadhi Yoga Studio in Budapest, Hungary, in Ádám Diószegi's teacher training.

In Budapest I taught weekly group classes in three districts — at the Buda Perinatal Center, the Prána Yoga Center and Korall Sportsziget — alongside online classes, outdoor yoga, live-music flows with handpan and tongue drum, sound yoga with guided meditation, and hatha flow and meditation sessions at the MANAS Festival. I also teach office yoga and team-building classes for companies, and mobility sessions for athletes.

Now I'm bringing the same practice to Fort Myers and Southwest Florida — to group classes, to lanais and clubhouses, and to the beach at sunrise.

How I teach

Dynamic, yet gentle. I build every class so a beginner can follow and someone who has practiced for years still enjoys it. I love the flow state — for me it's the most beautiful part of yoga — and sometimes I hold strengthening poses a little longer so everyone's attention can arrive.

You may meet a challenge in my classes, but nothing is compulsory. Nobody will look at you because you're not flexible, or because you're not yet where the person on the next mat is — or the teacher, or whoever you saw in a beautiful photo.

Awareness: I notice, I see, I observe, I allow — then I respond. Control: I want to steer it, grip it, regulate it, push it down. That is the most important difference yoga has taught me so far.

I'm proud that so many of my students come back week after week — people who resonate with this way of practicing and who are open to yoga as a whole, not just as a set of poses.

What yoga changed for me

From my own experience, and from what students have shared with me, regular practice can help loosen patterns like these:

  • a constant need to meet everyone's expectations, including your own
  • overthinking, and a mind that won't switch off at night
  • anxiety that plays the worst-case scenario on repeat
  • “stress addiction” — feeling useless unless you're busy
  • feeling empty or restless in your own company
  • losing touch with the world, burnout, the hamster wheel
  • fear of feeling your own emotions, or of trying something new
  • low self-confidence

Yoga isn't therapy and I'm not a doctor. But I've watched it give people room to breathe around all of these — myself included.

Already active — running, lifting, tennis, pickleball, paddleboarding? Hatha Flow will challenge you and give you back mobility.

Private Yoga in Fort Myers

One-on-one yoga at your home, lanai, condo clubhouse, on the beach or online — planned around your body and your goals.

✺

A class that fits exactly one person

In a group class I teach to the room. In a private session I teach to you: your shoulders after years at a desk, the knee you're careful with, the golf swing you'd like back, the sleep you'd like to find. We work at your pace, and every session builds on the last.

Who private yoga is for

  • Complete beginners who want to learn the foundations safely before joining a group
  • Anyone who prefers to practice without an audience
  • People working around stiffness, old injuries or limited mobility — with their doctor's OK
  • Couples, friends and families who want to practice together
  • Busy people who'd rather yoga came to them
  • Visitors and seasonal residents who want a sunrise session during their stay

Where we can practice

At home or on your lanai. All we need is a quiet spot the size of a yoga mat — or two, if you'd like to practice with a partner. I can bring mats and props.

On the beach. Sunrise and sunset sessions on the sand around Fort Myers Beach, Sanibel, Bonita Beach or your local stretch of the Gulf. In the summer months, early mornings are cooler and calmer.

In your condo or HOA clubhouse. A private group class for your community, one-off or weekly.

Online. Live, one-on-one video sessions — useful when you travel, or between in-person classes.

How it works

  1. Send a message with your area and the days that suit you.
  2. We talk for 15 minutes about how you move, any injuries or conditions, and what you'd like to feel after a class.
  3. Your first session. I bring a plan and adjust it as we go. You'll leave with one or two simple practices to do on your own.
  4. Keep going with single sessions or a 5-session pack — weekly, or whenever it suits you.

Sessions and prices

Private sessions are 60, 75 or 90 minutes. You'll find current rates on the schedule and pricing page.

Corporate & Athlete Yoga

Office yoga, team-building sessions, lunchtime classes and yoga for athletes and sports teams across Southwest Florida.

✺

Office yoga and team building

If you'd like to improve your team's focus, stress management and mental resilience — or you're simply a group of people who love yoga — let's plan something memorable together. A one-off team-building session, a weekly class alongside lunch, or short desk-friendly resets built into the working day.

Formats

  • Team-building session: 60–90 minutes, any fitness level, on-site or outdoors.
  • Weekly lunchtime class: 45–60 minutes, in a meeting room or on the lawn.
  • Chair and desk yoga: 20–30 minute resets for neck, shoulders and back. No mats, no changing clothes.
  • Retreats and offsites: sunrise flows or evening wind-downs for your event.

What teams usually notice

Less stiffness from long hours at a screen, easier breathing under pressure, and a shared calm that carries into meetings. And it's simply a good hour spent together.

Yoga for athletes and sports teams

If you'd like to improve your team's or your athletes' mobility, concentration, stress management, breathing and endurance, let's add yoga to training — with a strength, mobility or recovery focus — so everyone can bring 100% to the match, the race or the competition.

  • Mobility sessions for hips, shoulders and spine
  • Breathing practice for focus and faster recovery
  • Recovery classes after heavy training blocks
  • Pre-season and in-season programs

Yoga FAQ

Answers to the most common questions about classes, private yoga, beginners, payment and what to bring.

✺
Am I flexible enough for yoga?

You don't need to be flexible to start yoga — flexibility is something the practice builds. My classes are for people who, between work, family, grandkids, gardening and everything else, are perfectly happy with “that felt good,” “I've landed,” “I'm going to sleep so well” or “my back doesn't hurt anymore.”

We won't be practicing handstands. Classes are varied and there's always a little challenge in them, but nothing is compulsory.

I'm a complete beginner. Which class should I take?

Beginners are warmly welcome, especially if movement is already part of your life in some way. Slow Flow is the gentlest place to start; Hatha Flow is stronger and more dynamic. If you'd like to learn the foundations first, one or two private sessions are a great way in.

How hard are the group classes?

Everyone finds something different hard. For some it's the strength work, for others the stretching or the balance — and for some, switching off their thoughts for an hour.

Hatha Flow is the stronger, more dynamic class. Slow Flow puts more emphasis on observation, at a slower pace. Both include a flow experience, which for me is the most beautiful part of yoga. Sometimes I hold strengthening poses a little longer so everyone's attention can arrive.

What is hatha yoga?

“Ha” means sun and “tha” means moon. Hatha yoga balances the active and the passive energies in us: effort and ease, strength and surrender. Think of all the opposite poles that balance each other — hot and cold, light and shadow, receiving and letting go. One doesn't exist without the other.

When that balance tips, we feel it first as discomfort or restlessness. Hatha yoga uses physical practice to find and keep the balance. The poses (asanas) are a doorway to meditation — a more dynamic doorway — and only one of the eight limbs of yoga.

What should I bring?

Comfortable clothes you can move in, a bottle of water, and your own mat if you have a favorite. If you need to borrow one, mention it when you book. We practice barefoot. For beach sessions, bring a large towel or a mat, and sun protection.

Where do private yoga sessions take place?

Wherever suits you: your home or lanai, your condo or HOA clubhouse, your office, the beach — or online. I teach private sessions across Fort Myers and nearby areas including Cape Coral, Fort Myers Beach, Sanibel, Estero and Bonita Springs.

Do you offer beach yoga in Fort Myers?

Yes. Sunrise and sunset sessions on the sand are available as private sessions for individuals, couples and groups, and from time to time as group events. In summer, early mornings are the most comfortable; if a storm rolls in, we reschedule.

How can I pay?

You can pay by card when you book online, or in cash at class. Private sessions and passes can also be paid in advance.

Can I give yoga as a gift?

Yes — there are gift cards for a single class or a 5-class pass. After buying, send me the recipient's name, their email address for booking, and the class they'd enjoy. I'll make out the gift card in their name so you can forward or print it.

Do you teach yoga for companies and sports teams?

Yes: team-building sessions, weekly lunchtime classes, chair and desk yoga, and strength, mobility or recovery-focused yoga for athletes and sports teams. Send your team size and location for a proposal.

I have an injury or a health condition, or I'm pregnant. Can I join?

Please check with your doctor first, and tell me before class. In a group class I'll offer options; for specific needs, a private session is often the best way to start. Yoga complements medical care — it doesn't replace it.

What can a regular yoga practice help with?

Many people come to the mat for back and lower-back tension from sitting, a stiff “phone neck” and slumped posture, restless sleep, constant tiredness, a foggy mind, weak back and core muscles, or stress. Regular hatha practice builds deep strength, supports better posture and teaches you to use your breath more consciously — and many students find they sleep and focus better. If you have a medical condition, talk to your doctor about what's right for you.

Hatha Flow

The stronger, more dynamic side of my teaching: breath-led sequences, held strength poses, balance work and a flow you can lose yourself in.

60 minAll levels with some movement backgroundIntensity: Dynamic
✺

What happens in a Hatha Flow class

We begin by arriving — a few minutes of breath to leave the day at the door. Then we build heat: sun salutations, standing sequences, strength work for the deep muscles of the core, back and legs, and balance poses that ask for focus. Some poses flow with the breath; some we hold a little longer so everyone's attention can land.

The last part of class slows down: stretching, a few moments of stillness and a long relaxation.

Who it's for

Hatha Flow is the stronger, more dynamic class. It suits you if movement is already part of your life in some way — walking, the gym, tennis, pickleball, golf, paddleboarding — and you're comfortable getting down to the floor and back up. You don't need to be flexible.

What you'll take home

  • Strength in the deep core and back muscles that support good posture
  • More freedom in your hips, shoulders and spine
  • Steadier balance and focus
  • A breath you can use when the day gets loud

Slow Flow

Slower and more observant. We still flow, but with time to feel each shape — ideal after a long day and for beginners.

75–90 minBeginners welcomeIntensity: Gentle
✺

A slower class with more room to notice

Slow Flow still moves — the flow experience matters to me in every class — but the pace leaves space to feel each shape, to notice where you're holding on, and to let go a little. There's more time on the floor, more stretching and a longer relaxation.

Who it's for

Complete beginners, anyone returning after a break, people who sit a lot, and anyone who ends the day both wired and tired. Experienced practitioners love it too, as a counterweight to stronger training.

What to expect

  • Gentle breathwork to arrive
  • Mobility for the spine, hips and shoulders
  • Slow, mindful standing and balance work
  • Longer-held floor stretches
  • A guided relaxation to close

Private Yoga in Fort Myers: What a One-on-One Session Is Really Like

What happens in a private yoga session, who it helps most, and how to get the most out of practicing one-on-one at home, on your lanai or on the beach.

September 22, 20262 min readPrivate yoga
✺

Most people picture private yoga as something for celebrities or advanced practitioners. In reality, the people who book one-on-one sessions with me in Fort Myers are usually the opposite: beginners who don't want to feel lost in a room full of experienced yogis, busy people who can't make a fixed class time, and anyone who wants their practice to answer to their own body rather than to the average of a group.

Before the first session: a short conversation

Every private series starts with a 15-minute call. I ask how you move day to day, whether there's anything to be careful with — a shoulder, a knee, a lower back that complains after a long drive — and what you'd like to feel after a class. Calmer? Stronger? Less stiff on the golf course? That conversation shapes everything that follows.

The session itself

We start by arriving: a few minutes of breathing, so the part of you still answering emails can catch up with the part standing on the mat. Then we move. Unlike a group class, I can slow down exactly where you need it, repeat what you want to learn, and skip what doesn't serve you. If a pose doesn't work for your body, we find the version that does.

Most sessions end with a relaxation long enough to actually relax, and with one or two short practices you can do on your own between sessions.

Where it happens

This is where Southwest Florida makes private yoga special. Sessions can take place in your living room, on a screened lanai, in your condo clubhouse, or on the sand at sunrise. All we need is a quiet space about the size of a yoga mat. I can bring mats and props, so there's nothing to buy before you start.

Who benefits most

  • Beginners who want to learn the foundations safely before joining a group class.
  • People with stiffness or old injuries who need a pace and a plan of their own (with their doctor's OK).
  • Couples and friends who want a shared hour that isn't another dinner out.
  • Seasonal residents and visitors who want a few sunrise sessions during their stay.

How often?

Once a week is a wonderful rhythm: enough to feel real change within a month, especially if you add ten minutes of practice on a couple of other days. Some students book a pack of five, others come whenever their schedule allows. There's no wrong way.

If you're curious, read how private yoga works or simply send me a message with your area and the days that suit you.

Hatha Flow vs. Slow Flow: Which Yoga Class Is Right for You?

Both classes include breath, strength, stretching, balance and relaxation. Here is how they differ — and how to choose between them.

September 15, 20261 min readPractice
✺

“Which class should I come to?” is the question I hear most often from new students in Fort Myers. There are countless styles of yoga, and the names don't always help. So here's a plain-language guide to the two group classes I teach.

What they have in common

Both are hatha yoga. Both include breathing exercises, strengthening, stretching, balance, a flow experience and a proper relaxation at the end. In both, you'll find options to make things easier or more challenging — and in both, nothing is compulsory.

Hatha Flow: the dynamic one

Hatha Flow represents the stronger, more dynamic side of the practice. We link movement and breath into flowing sequences, build heat, and sometimes hold strengthening poses a little longer so attention has time to settle. You'll work the deep core and back muscles that support your posture, and leave feeling both energized and quiet.

Choose Hatha Flow if movement is already part of your life — gym, running, tennis, pickleball, paddleboarding, long walks — and you'd like a class that challenges you while giving back mobility.

Slow Flow: the observant one

Slow Flow keeps the flow but slows everything down. The emphasis moves from effort to observation: noticing how a shape feels, where you're gripping, what happens when you let go a little. There's more floor work, more stretching and a longer rest.

Choose Slow Flow if you're new to yoga, returning after a break, sitting a lot, or finishing your days tired and wired at the same time. It's also a perfect counterweight to hard training.

Still not sure?

Ask yourself one question: do you need more energy, or more calm? If energy, try Hatha Flow. If calm, try Slow Flow. And if you'd rather learn the basics with full attention first, one or two private sessions make joining a group much easier.

You'll find both on the weekly schedule. Come as you are — nobody on the next mat is watching.

Sunrise Beach Yoga Around Fort Myers: How to Make It Feel Amazing

Practical tips for practicing yoga on the sand in Southwest Florida — timing, heat, tides, what to bring and how to make the most of it.

September 7, 20262 min readBeach yoga
✺

There are few better places to practice yoga than a Southwest Florida beach before the day heats up. The sand is cool, the Gulf is often glassy, and the pelicans are already at work. Here's how to make a beach session feel as good as it looks.

Go early (or late)

From late spring to early fall, the first hour after sunrise is the sweet spot: cooler air, softer light, fewer people. Because our Gulf beaches face west, the sun rises behind you — which means gentle light on your back rather than glare in your eyes. Sunset sessions are beautiful too, with the sun going down over the water, but the sand holds the day's heat longer.

Choose your spot

Fort Myers Beach, Sanibel, Lovers Key and Bonita Beach all have long stretches of sand. Look for firm, flat sand just above the high-tide line: dry enough to stay put, firm enough for balance poses. Check the tide times before you go so the water doesn't join the class. If you're planning an organized group session in a park or preserve, check the local rules first.

What to bring

  • A large towel or an old mat (sand gets everywhere — don't bring your favorite)
  • Water, even at 7am
  • Reef-safe sunscreen and a hat for the way back
  • A light layer for the final relaxation on breezy mornings

Adjust your practice to the sand

Sand is unstable, which makes balance poses both harder and more rewarding. Widen your stance a little, move more slowly, and let your feet work — they'll thank you. Keep flows gentle and save the strongest standing work for the studio. Lying down at the end and listening to the waves is the best relaxation you'll ever have.

Want company?

I teach sunrise and sunset sessions on the beach as private yoga for individuals, couples, families and groups — and from time to time as open events. It's a lovely way to start a vacation, celebrate a birthday or simply reset a busy week.
